## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## claude.ai Firecrawl
Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Firecrawl provides web, developer, government, and research search, and executes catalogued Alexandria data providers. Use firecrawl_search to find relevant results across the web and specialized indexes; authenticated searches also return matching Alexandria providers in data.tools. firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and provider contracts; firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_scrape with a url retrieves one supplied page. For a programming question, firecrawl_developer_search searches indexed public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, READMEs, and code documentation and returns the matched passages, and skills: "only" narrows it to agent-skill files; firecrawl_search with categories: ["developer"] reaches the same index beside ordinary web results, returning the hits in the web group rather than as passages and offering no skills filter. For a legal or regulatory question, firecrawl_gov_search searches primary law and regulatory material from US federal, state, and local government sources: statutes, regulations, codes, court opinions, and other government publications; firecrawl_search with categories: ["gov"] reaches the same sources in the web group and cannot be combined with other categories. For a biomedical, life-science, clinical, or arXiv literature question, the firecrawl_research_* tools search the paper index, while categories: ["research"] on firecrawl_search filters ordinary web results to research-affiliated websites. Use the firecrawl_research_* tools to search academic and research literature, expand from anchor papers via the citation graph, and read full-text passages from a specific paper. Search and discovery tools are read-only and return ranked results. Billing: web, developer, and research search are billed per request; government search is free; Alexandria discovery (firecrawl_search with sources ["alexandria"] alone, and firecrawl_find_tools) is free; firecrawl_scrape is billed, as a page retrieval in url mode or at each executed capability's listed price in alexandria mode.

# Browser Use

Direct browser control via CDP. For task-specific edits, use `agent-workspace/agent_helpers.py`. For setup, install, or connection problems, read https://github.com/browser-use/browser-harness/blob/main/install.md.

## When Not to Use

A basic fetch of public information needs no browser. If a plain HTTP request can read it — a public page, an API, docs — use `curl` or your fetch tool, and leave the browser alone. Use browser-use when the task needs interaction (click, type, navigate), the user's logged-in session, JS rendering, or a bot-protected page. If a direct fetch fails or returns a shell page, then escalate to the browser.

Domain skills are off by default. Set `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` to enable them; see the bottom section.

**If `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` and the task is site-specific, read every file in the matching `$BH_AGENT_WORKSPACE/domain-skills/<site>/` directory before inventing an approach.**

## Usage

```bash
browser-use <<'PY'
print(page_info())
PY
```

- Invoke as `browser-use`. Use heredocs for multi-line commands.
- Helpers are pre-imported. `run.py` calls `ensure_daemon()` before `exec`.
- First navigation for a task is `new_tab(url)`, not `goto_url(url)`. The daemon
  preserves the attached tab across separate CLI invocations, so do not call
  `new_tab()` again in every script.
- Keep one working tab per task/site. Before opening another, inspect
  `current_tab()` and `list_tabs()` and use `switch_tab()` to reuse a matching
  tab. Do not leave duplicate tabs on the same URL or close tabs you did not
  create.
- At task completion, close tabs created for the task that are no longer needed.
  Keep a tab open if the user needs to see it, it is needed for a known follow-up,
  or closing it could discard unsaved work or other important state.
- `new_tab()` and `switch_tab()` attach and move the horse marker without
  changing Chrome's visible tab. Screenshots and normal CDP input work in the
  background. Never call `activate_tab(target)` automatically: it brings Chrome
  to the foreground. Call it only when the user explicitly asks to see or
  visibly switch to that tab. Do not pair `switch_tab()` with `activate_tab()`.
- A local daemon is a connection to the whole Chrome instance, not to one site,
  task, card, or agent. Omit `BU_NAME` and reuse the default daemon for normal
  sequential local work across websites, tabs, screenshots, and Codex turns.
  Do not invent per-job names such as `gmail1375` or `slack1371`: every new
  local daemon opens another browser-level CDP connection and Chrome may show
  another Allow prompt.
- Set `BH_TAB_MARKER=0` before starting the daemon to leave page titles unchanged.
  The horse marker remains enabled by default.
- A timeout or page that pauses while hidden is not permission to foreground
  Chrome. Keep using background CDP operations. For a focus-gated page,
  temporarily call `cdp("Emulation.setFocusEmulationEnabled", enabled=True)`,
  perform and verify the operation, then disable it in a `finally` block. If
  background control still cannot work, report that limitation instead of
  activating the tab. Do not invent a `Runtime.evaluate` scroll replacement or
  a cross-frame JS walker.
- The normal local flow attaches to the running Chrome/Chromium CDP endpoint. No browser ids or local profile selection.

# Browser Use

Direct browser control via CDP. For task-specific edits, use `agent-workspace/agent_helpers.py`. For setup, install, or connection problems, read https://github.com/browser-use/browser-harness/blob/main/install.md.

## When Not to Use

A basic fetch of public information needs no browser. If a plain HTTP request can read it — a public page, an API, docs — use `curl` or your fetch tool, and leave the browser alone. Use browser-use when the task needs interaction (click, type, navigate), the user's logged-in session, JS rendering, or a bot-protected page. If a direct fetch fails or returns a shell page, then escalate to the browser.

Domain skills are off by default. Set `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` to enable them; see the bottom section.

**If `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` and the task is site-specific, read every file in the matching `$BH_AGENT_WORKSPACE/domain-skills/<site>/` directory before inventing an approach.**

## Usage

```bash
browser-use <<'PY'
print(page_info())
PY
```

- Invoke as `browser-use`. Use heredocs for multi-line commands.
- Helpers are pre-imported. `run.py` calls `ensure_daemon()` before `exec`.
- First navigation for a task is `new_tab(url)`, not `goto_url(url)`. The daemon
  preserves the attached tab across separate CLI invocations, so do not call
  `new_tab()` again in every script.
- Keep one working tab per task/site. Before opening another, inspect
  `current_tab()` and `list_tabs()` and use `switch_tab()` to reuse a matching
  tab. Do not leave duplicate tabs on the same URL or close tabs you did not
  create.
- At task completion, close tabs created for the task that are no longer needed.
  Keep a tab open if the user needs to see it, it is needed for a known follow-up,
  or closing it could discard unsaved work or other important state.
- `new_tab()` and `switch_tab()` attach and move the horse marker without
  changing Chrome's visible tab. Screenshots and normal CDP input work in the
  background. Never call `activate_tab(target)` automatically: it brings Chrome
  to the foreground. Call it only when the user explicitly asks to see or
  visibly switch to that tab. Do not pair `switch_tab()` with `activate_tab()`.
- A local daemon is a connection to the whole Chrome instance, not to one site,
  task, card, or agent. Omit `BU_NAME` and reuse the default daemon for normal
  sequential local work across websites, tabs, screenshots, and Codex turns.
  Do not invent per-job names such as `gmail1375` or `slack1371`: every new
  local daemon opens another browser-level CDP connection and Chrome may show
  another Allow prompt.
- Set `BH_TAB_MARKER=0` before starting the daemon to leave page titles unchanged.
  The horse marker remains enabled by default.
- A timeout or page that pauses while hidden is not permission to foreground
  Chrome. Keep using background CDP operations. For a focus-gated page,
  temporarily call `cdp("Emulation.setFocusEmulationEnabled", enabled=True)`,
  perform and verify the operation, then disable it in a `finally` block. If

  activating the tab. Do not invent a `Runtime.evaluate` scroll replacement or
  a cross-frame JS walker.

# AGENTS.md

Project: Flint

## What this is
Flint is Claude working as Eric's sport-science, performance, S&C and rehab thought
partner. This repo builds the knowledge base behind that role. It catalogs Eric's
Drive (his own material, TB's Training Info, Landon Evans, courses, papers), routes the
high-value sources into Zotero and the SecondBrain vault, and writes per-discipline
synthesis notes that compare the sources against Eric's own method. It is a side-lane
project, outside the prioritization-slate cap. See `README.md` for the approach and
`docs/PLAN.md` for the checklist.

## Session routine
- Start: run `git pull`, then read docs/STATUS.md before doing anything else.
- End: update docs/STATUS.md (done, next, open questions), commit, and `git push`.
- Never leave uncommitted work at the end of a session.

## Conventions
- Durable notes and decisions go in docs/, committed. Not in chat, not in cloud project docs.
- Documents, data exports, and deliverables live on the primary storage drive (Google Drive 00_Primary_Storage_Drive), not in the repo. Files over 95 MB never go in git.
- `data/` is gitignored except aggregate summaries. Regenerate the file-level manifest with `pwsh scripts/build_manifest.ps1`.
- Codex workers read staged copies in `staging/`, never the Drive root. DexaProject, athlete snapshots, Catapult and PFF exports are never catalogued.
- The ingest review gate has two stages.
  1. Before atomizing, verify the source artifact by an independent route: page order, scanned versus text, transcripts checked against captions.
  2. Before promoting, Codex reviews the staged entries against the staged sources, with instructions to falsify (`staging/review_<source>_codex.md`). Nothing reaches the vault without a GO or a GO AFTER FIXES that has been applied.
- Library entries label every voice. The source author's statements are plain. Eric's judgments get "Eric's review:". The entry writer's own reasoning gets "Inference:". No unlabeled judgments. Every number carries a timestamp or page the reviewer can check, and a claim is only tagged "confirmed in PDF" if that PDF is staged. (Learned from the Harries review, 2026-09-26: 25 of 35 files needed fixes, mostly for attribution.)
- Writing: plain, direct, no em dashes. Documents use the Baylor design system.

24:**Example** — The author applies item 3 at once to the vertical jump: because results "correlate best with conditions which are most similar to that of the test", it is "useful to repeat the test with the non-dominant hand or in the frontal plane with the athlete using both hands" (PDF 468 / p.457). See [[heuristic--vertical-jump-test-five-start-conditions-and-knee-angle-profile]].
---
20:**When to apply** — When a single jump number cannot say why an athlete jumps what they jump. Eric's review: "The standard CMJ family run on ForceDecks: hands-free squat, squat jump (quarter-squat start, 3s hold), countermovement jump (x3), hop test / repeated CMJ (10 reps total, n=5 pairs), and single-leg CMJ (x3 per leg)" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 77, Inferred (protocol; author uncertain); the line goes on to say each test has a scripted weigh-in, stabilization and rep protocol). Inference: the squat jump with a 3 s hold is close to the book's condition 1, and the CMJ to condition 4 or 5; the quoted line does not say whether arms are used in the CMJ. Eric's review: the DSI is used "to determine whether we need more plyometric training or more max-strength training" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 76, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q21)), and the same line tags that use "[contested; the ratio tracks IMTP strength; one controlled trial (Pleša 2024, basketball, split at 0.90) supported only the strength arm; no football data]". Inference: the book's static-versus-dip contrast is a field cousin of that decision, and it carries the same caution.
22:**When NOT to apply** — The book gives no norms, no data and no rule for which result means which training: it says the contrast "can sometimes assist one in ascertaining" the need, nothing more. Do not import a direction from Ch 1, where the book gives two conflicting rules for the static-versus-dip gap ([[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]]). Inference: "a fairly large knee angle" is ambiguous, since the book does not say how the angle is measured; its link to "a slower overall jumping time" suggests a deeper start, but that is a reading, not the text. The book's "optimum" and "optimal" start positions are not defined.
24:**Example** — The book's own reasoning for an athlete who jumps best from a deep static start (the large knee angle case above): the jump takes longer from start to finish, and the book says that athlete should work on the "range and speed of maximal strength production" (PDF 469 / p.458).
---
16:**What it is** — Under "Muscle Strength Ratios" the book takes on "the most commonly quoted" agonist-antagonist ratio, "the 60:40 ratio of knee extension to knee flexion strength (i.e. extensors 1.5 times stronger than flexors)," and refers back to Section 4.2.6.2 for its limitations (PDF 469 / p.458, checked against the page image). It adds that "these ratios not only vary with joint angle, joint velocity and type of movement, but also with muscle group and the type of athlete." Its data (Vorobyev, 1978): "the relative isometric strength (per 1kg bodymass) of the larger extensor muscles in Olympic weightlifters is 11.51 ± 1.78, and for the major flexors it is 4.02 ± 0.69 ... In general, their major extensors are on average 2.86 times stronger than their major flexors, a figure which is very different from the isokinetic value of 1.5 cited by sports physiotherapists for the average person (whatever this entity might be)" (PDF 469-470 / pp.458-459; "In general" and "different" sit on the compressed right margin of PDF 469 and are partly reconstructed). By region, "Among the best Russian weightlifters the relative maximum strength of extensors to flexors is as follows: arms 1.6:1, trunk 4.3:1, thighs 4.3:1, and lower leg 5.4:1" (PDF 470 / p.459). The conclusion: "The application of these findings on their own to sport or rehabilitation is incomplete and must be accompanied by the profile of strength produced at important joint angles in every given sport, in accordance with the principle of dynamic correspondence, especially the accentuated region of force production (Section 4.3)" (PDF 470 / p.459).
22:**When NOT to apply** — The 2.86 figure is isometric and for weightlifters; the 1.5 it is set against is isokinetic and for "the average person," so the book compares two different measures, which is part of its point. Inference: the 4.2.6.2 entry reports Vorobyev's isokinetic knee ratio of "nearer 80:20 for weightlifters" ([[heuristic--isokinetic-strength-ratios-vary-by-angle-and-velocity]]); 80:20 is 4:1, close to the thigh ratio of 4.3:1 here, and different in kind from the whole-body 2.86. These are different measurements, not a conflict, so not `contested`. No sample sizes, test positions or "larger extensor" and "major flexor" muscle lists are given. Weightlifter ratios are not targets for other sports.
26:**Related** — [[heuristic--isokinetic-strength-ratios-vary-by-angle-and-velocity]], [[heuristic--train-force-at-the-accentuated-joint-angle]]
---
16:**What it is** — Under "Work Capacity and Functional Pressure Tests," which the book calls "an extension" of the Ch 6.2.2 tests, it describes "the cardiac function Shtanga Functional Pressure test to ascertain if the athlete is overtraining (described by Vyurberg, 1953)," regarded as "particularly suitable for athletes like Olympic weightlifters and wrestlers, whose sports require them to strain against heavy resistance" (PDF 470 / p.459, checked against the page image). Procedure: breathe in relaxed fashion for a few minutes, inhale maximally, hold "for 15-20 seconds before stopping the nose and exhaling as forcibly as possible for 2 seconds," which brings "a sharp rise in intrathoracic pressure and diminished flow of blood to the heart." Blood pressure is taken before (BP1), immediately after (BP2) and after 2 minutes of relaxed breathing (BP3). "If the contractile processes of the myocardium are normal, as in the well-prepared athlete who is not exhibiting chronic fatigue, the blood pressure decreases briefly by 5-10mm Hg." Ulchenko (1982) used it "among elite weightlifters during their specific preparation stage": Test 1, the three readings before training; Test 2, the same readings "during the most intense training loading." Grades: "1. BP decrease after Test 1 or no change after Test 2. This is regarded as an excellent reaction. 2. BP increase of up to 5mm Hg immediately after Test 2 and recovery of normal BP after 2 minutes rest. This is considered to be a good reaction. 3. BP increase of up to 7mm Hg after Test 2 and 5 minutes recovery time. This is regarded as satisfactory. 4. BP increase of 10mm Hg or more after Test 2 and prolonged elevation of BP afterwards. This is regarded as an unsatisfactory response and is associated with an overtraining state" (PDF 470 / p.459). One lifter who "reported feeling fit and strong" with low RPE scored: Test 1, BP1 130/70, BP2 140/75, BP3 135/70, a 10 mm rise "regarded as unsatisfactory"; Test 2, BP1 140/66, BP2 160/70, BP3 142/70, a 20 mm rise, also unsatisfactory. "This lifter and several others whose pressure tests were deemed to be unacceptable did not improve their results in the competition which followed," and their coaches were advised to modify training "until the pressure tests indicated a better functional state" (PDF 470 / p.459). Heavy supplementary resistance training ("cross training") serves this, "provided that it does not alter the neuromuscular patterns needed in the given sport." content.content:
**Why it works** — Strength testing and training programs typically control for load,
volume, and technique, but this list makes explicit that psychological state, injury
history, and perceived pain/fear operate as real physiological limiters on force output.
Reflex inhibition around an injured joint is stated in the text as "a well-known phenomenon
which produces muscle weakness when a joint is damaged" (Stokes & Young, 1984; printed 14).
Inference: this is not just a "mental" factor layered on top of a physical ceiling, but a
measurable neuromuscular effect, not a motivation problem.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** usable as a checklist when an athlete's force output
underperforms their apparent physical capacity: before assuming a physical/programming
cause, rule out fear of re-injury, unaddressed effort-pain tolerance, or psychological
state. The authors state "return to top level performance will occur only if the
athlete perceives rehabilitation to be complete" and the fear of pain or re-injury being
minimal (PDF p. 25, printed p. 14). **Eric's baseline:** Applied Performance's stated role
in return-to-performance is to supply information supporting Athletic Performance's and
Athletic Medicine's RTP decisions, a support/advisory role rather than a final-decision
role (`method-baseline.md`, "Rehab and return to play," citing
`baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.6`); that same baseline section is flagged as
"the thinnest discipline in the corpus" with no stated RTP criteria or battery.
**Inference:** the authors' fear-of-injury/pain framing is a plausible partial fill for
that documented gap, though neither source states this connection directly.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a descriptive taxonomy, not a measurement
protocol; none of these seven factors have a given cutoff or test threshold in this section
of the text (PDF pp. 23-25, printed pp. 12-14). **Inference:** do not use "fear of injury"
as a catch-all explanation without other supporting evidence (movement quality, self-report,
clinical input from Athletic Medicine); reflex inhibition and psychological guarding can
look similar from the outside. This caution is this entry's own judgment, not stated in the
text.

**Example** — **Inference:** An athlete cleared medically after an ACL reconstruction who still shows
reduced force output on the operated leg during testing may be exhibiting reflex inhibition
and/or fear of re-injury, not a residual physical deficit alone; that changes what the
next intervention should target.

**Related** — [[framework--central-vs-peripheral-fatigue-mechanisms]].

# McDougall's Four Values of Testing and Seven Characteristics of an Effective Testing Programme

**What it is** — Section 8.7 opens by restating that "the most specific test of all is performance in the actual sporting event. All other tests have varying degrees of correlation with performance or selected actions in the given sport" (PDF 468 / p.457, checked against the page image). The author, writing in the first person ("my Canadian colleague, Dr Duncan Mc Dougall"), then summarises McDougall et al (1982). Four values of "suitable, well-planned tests": (1) "They identify individual strengths and weaknesses and provide data for determining the baseline for training programmes"; (2) "They provide feedback on the effectiveness of training programmes"; (3) "They provide information on the athlete's state of health"; (4) "They provide an educational process which teaches the athlete to understand more competently his/her body and the demands of the sport." Seven characteristics of an effective programme: (1) "The variables which are tested must be directly relevant to the given sport"; (2) "The tests must be valid (test what it claims to), reliable and reproducible"; (3) "The testing procedures must be as sport specific as possible"; (4) "The testing situation must be rigidly controlled"; (5) "Testing must be repeated at regular, appropriate intervals"; (6) "The tests must respect the athlete's human rights (including ethics, confidentiality and risks)"; (7) "The results must be interpreted in understandable language directly to the athlete and coach" (PDF 468 / p.457). The author then says the section will not "reiterate what has already been written" by testing authorities and will "simply ... provide information which is not readily available" (PDF 468 / p.457). The book prints the name both as "Mc Dougall" and "McDougall"; the OCR's "Me Dougall" is an artifact.

**Why it works** — The book gives no separate mechanism; the lists rest on the opening point that every test other than competition is only a correlate of performance. Inference: items 1 and 3 keep that correlate as close to the sport as possible; items 2, 4 and 5 make a change between two test dates attributable to training rather than to noise or a changed protocol; item 7 makes the result usable by the people who change the programme.

**When to apply** — When building or auditing a test battery, or deciding whether to keep a test. Eric's review: "If it doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need, then it doesn't have a place." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 32, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q3)). Eric's review: "Testing protocol has to be exactly repeatable over time ("how you do it in January needs to be the same as how you do it in April") or the resulting data cannot be trusted for comparison." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 57, Inferred (transcript)). Eric's review: "Inconsistent data from a good test is still bad data" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 34, Explicit). Inference: McDougall's items 1, 4 and 5 match these lines; the baseline lines quoted here say nothing about item 6 (ethics and confidentiality) or item 7 (explaining results directly to the athlete).

**When NOT to apply** — The lists are a checklist, not evidence that testing improves results; McDougall et al (1982) is cited, not described, so `untested`. Inference: items 1 and 3 ("as sport specific as possible") pull against item 2 (reliability), since the most sport-like tests are often the hardest to control; Eric's own battery leans on general, reliable tests ("bodyweight, 60-yard dash, vertical jump, broad jump, back squat, push-up max", `docs/method-baseline.md`, line 58). The four values say what tests can "provide", not that every test must serve all four.

**Example** — The author applies item 3 at once to the vertical jump: because results "correlate best with conditions which are most similar to that of the test", it is "useful to repeat the test with the non-dominant hand or in the frontal plane with the athlete using both hands" (PDF 468 / p.457). See [[heuristic--vertical-jump-test-five-start-conditions-and-knee-angle-profile]].

# Run the Vertical Jump Under Several Start Conditions and Knee Angles, Not One

**What it is** — The usual vertical jump has the athlete "leap from a standing position with a preliminary dip and touch a measuring device sideways with one's dominant hand" (PDF 468 / p.457, checked against the page image). Because "the results of this test correlate best with conditions which are most similar to that of the test," the book advises repeating it "with the non-dominant hand or in the frontal plane with the athlete using both hands to reach for the target." It lists five start conditions: "1. Starting statically from an optimum knee flexed position using no arm swing; 2. Starting statically from an optimum knee flexed position using arm swing; 3. Starting statically from sitting on a low seat using (a) no arm swing, or (b) arm swing; 4. Starting dynamically with an optimal knee dip using no arm swing; 5. Starting dynamically with an optimal knee dip using arm swing" (PDF 468 / p.457). Two contrasts are drawn. Without arm swing the jump focuses "primarily on the role played by extension of the lower extremity and trunk, without the picture being confounded by the use of arm momentum." Without the dip, "the absence of an initial sharp dip allows one to focus more on starting strength and the role played by the contractile (actin-myosin) component of the muscle complex, instead of the more plyometric rebound action encouraged by the use of the dip. This can sometimes assist one in ascertaining whether the athlete needs more strength (or functional hypertrophy) training or more rebound, nervous system training" (PDF 468-469 / pp.457-458). Static jumps can also be run "from different initial knee angles to obtain a profile of individual jumping characteristics": "if the maximum vertical jump is attained for a fairly large knee angle, which is generally associated with a slower overall jumping time from start to finish of the action, then it is obvious that the athlete needs to concentrate on modifying his range and speed of maximal strength production" (PDF 469 / p.458; "profile of", "knee" and "then it is" sit on the compressed right margin and are partly reconstructed from the image).

**Why it works** — The book's reasoning: each condition removes one contributor (arm momentum, the stretch-shortening rebound), so the difference between conditions points at the contributor. Inference: the static-versus-dip contrast is the same logic as the Ch 1 strength-deficit proxy, applied here as a diagnostic menu rather than a single comparison.

**When to apply** — When a single jump number cannot say why an athlete jumps what they jump. Eric's review: "The standard CMJ family run on ForceDecks: hands-free squat, squat jump (quarter-squat start, 3s hold), countermovement jump (x3), hop test / repeated CMJ (10 reps total, n=5 pairs), and single-leg CMJ (x3 per leg)" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 77, Inferred (protocol; author uncertain); the line goes on to say each test has a scripted weigh-in, stabilization and rep protocol). Inference: the squat jump with a 3 s hold is close to the book's condition 1, and the CMJ to condition 4 or 5; the quoted line does not say whether arms are used in the CMJ. Eric's review: the DSI is used "to determine whether we need more plyometric training or more max-strength training" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 76, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q21)), and the same line tags that use "[contested; the ratio tracks IMTP strength; one controlled trial (Pleša 2024, basketball, split at 0.90) supported only the strength arm; no football data]". Inference: the book's static-versus-dip contrast is a field cousin of that decision, and it carries the same caution.

**When NOT to apply** — The book gives no norms, no data and no rule for which result means which training: it says the contrast "can sometimes assist one in ascertaining" the need, nothing more. Do not import a direction from Ch 1, where the book gives two conflicting rules for the static-versus-dip gap ([[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]]). Inference: "a fairly large knee angle" is ambiguous, since the book does not say how the angle is measured; its link to "a slower overall jumping time" suggests a deeper start, but that is a reading, not the text. The book's "optimum" and "optimal" start positions are not defined.

**Example** — The book's own reasoning for an athlete who jumps best from a deep static start (the large knee angle case above): the jump takes longer from start to finish, and the book says that athlete should work on the "range and speed of maximal strength production" (PDF 469 / p.458).

# Weightlifters' Extensors Are About 2.9 Times Stronger Than Their Flexors, Far From the 1.5 "Norm"

**What it is** — Under "Muscle Strength Ratios" the book takes on "the most commonly quoted" agonist-antagonist ratio, "the 60:40 ratio of knee extension to knee flexion strength (i.e. extensors 1.5 times stronger than flexors)," and refers back to Section 4.2.6.2 for its limitations (PDF 469 / p.458, checked against the page image). It adds that "these ratios not only vary with joint angle, joint velocity and type of movement, but also with muscle group and the type of athlete." Its data (Vorobyev, 1978): "the relative isometric strength (per 1kg bodymass) of the larger extensor muscles in Olympic weightlifters is 11.51 ± 1.78, and for the major flexors it is 4.02 ± 0.69 ... In general, their major extensors are on average 2.86 times stronger than their major flexors, a figure which is very different from the isokinetic value of 1.5 cited by sports physiotherapists for the average person (whatever this entity might be)" (PDF 469-470 / pp.458-459; "In general" and "different" sit on the compressed right margin of PDF 469 and are partly reconstructed). By region, "Among the best Russian weightlifters the relative maximum strength of extensors to flexors is as follows: arms 1.6:1, trunk 4.3:1, thighs 4.3:1, and lower leg 5.4:1" (PDF 470 / p.459). The conclusion: "The application of these findings on their own to sport or rehabilitation is incomplete and must be accompanied by the profile of strength produced at important joint angles in every given sport, in accordance with the principle of dynamic correspondence, especially the accentuated region of force production (Section 4.3)" (PDF 470 / p.459).

**Why it works** — The book's reasoning is specificity: a ratio reflects the muscles a sport loads, so an athlete whose sport is dominated by extension will show high extensor-to-flexor ratios without being "imbalanced." Inference: 11.51 / 4.02 = 2.86, so the book's "2.86 times" is the ratio of the two group means.

**When to apply** — Before calling an athlete "imbalanced" from a ratio: check which athlete type, muscle group, joint angle, speed and contraction type the reference ratio came from. Then, as the book says, pair the ratio with the strength profile at the joint angles the sport uses (see [[heuristic--train-force-at-the-accentuated-joint-angle]]).

**When NOT to apply** — The 2.86 figure is isometric and for weightlifters; the 1.5 it is set against is isokinetic and for "the average person," so the book compares two different measures, which is part of its point. Inference: the 4.2.6.2 entry reports Vorobyev's isokinetic knee ratio of "nearer 80:20 for weightlifters" ([[heuristic--isokinetic-strength-ratios-vary-by-angle-and-velocity]]); 80:20 is 4:1, close to the thigh ratio of 4.3:1 here, and different in kind from the whole-body 2.86. These are different measurements, not a conflict, so not `contested`. No sample sizes, test positions or "larger extensor" and "major flexor" muscle lists are given. Weightlifter ratios are not targets for other sports.

**Example** — The lower leg shows the most extreme ratio among the best Russian weightlifters, 5.4:1, against 1.6:1 for the arms (PDF 470 / p.459).

**Related** — [[heuristic--isokinetic-strength-ratios-vary-by-angle-and-velocity]], [[heuristic--train-force-at-the-accentuated-joint-angle]]

# Weightlifters' Extensors Are About 2.9 Times Stronger Than Their Flexors, Far From the 1.5 "Norm"

**What it is** — Under "Muscle Strength Ratios" the book takes on "the most commonly quoted" agonist-antagonist ratio, "the 60:40 ratio of knee extension to knee flexion strength (i.e. extensors 1.5 times stronger than flexors)," and refers back to Section 4.2.6.2 for its limitations (PDF 469 / p.458, checked against the page image). It adds that "these ratios not only vary with joint angle, joint velocity and type of movement, but also with muscle group and the type of athlete." Its data (Vorobyev, 1978): "the relative isometric strength (per 1kg bodymass) of the larger extensor muscles in Olympic weightlifters is 11.51 ± 1.78, and for the major flexors it is 4.02 ± 0.69 ... In general, their major extensors are on average 2.86 times stronger than their major flexors, a figure which is very different from the isokinetic value of 1.5 cited by sports physiotherapists for the average person (whatever this entity might be)" (PDF 469-470 / pp.458-459; "In general" and "different" sit on the compressed right margin of PDF 469 and are partly reconstructed). By region, "Among the best Russian weightlifters the relative maximum strength of extensors to flexors is as follows: arms 1.6:1, trunk 4.3:1, thighs 4.3:1, and lower leg 5.4:1" (PDF 470 / p.459). The conclusion: "The application of these findings on their own to sport or rehabilitation is incomplete and must be accompanied by the profile of strength produced at important joint angles in every given sport, in accordance with the principle of dynamic correspondence, especially the accentuated region of force production (Section 4.3)" (PDF 470 / p.459).

**Why it works** — The book's reasoning is specificity: a ratio reflects the muscles a sport loads, so an athlete whose sport is dominated by extension will show high extensor-to-flexor ratios without being "imbalanced." Inference: 11.51 / 4.02 = 2.86, so the book's "2.86 times" is the ratio of the two group means.

**When to apply** — Before calling an athlete "imbalanced" from a ratio: check which athlete type, muscle group, joint angle, speed and contraction type the reference ratio came from. Then, as the book says, pair the ratio with the strength profile at the joint angles the sport uses (see [[heuristic--train-force-at-the-accentuated-joint-angle]]).

**When NOT to apply** — The 2.86 figure is isometric and for weightlifters; the 1.5 it is set against is isokinetic and for "the average person." Inference: so the book compares two different measures, which is part of its point; the book's stated point is that ratios vary by muscle group and athlete type. Inference: the 4.2.6.2 entry reports Vorobyev's knee ratio (measured at peak extension torque; mode not stated) of "nearer 80:20 for weightlifters" ([[heuristic--isokinetic-strength-ratios-vary-by-angle-and-velocity]]); 80:20 is 4:1, close to the thigh ratio of 4.3:1 here, and different in kind from the pooled major-extensor to major-flexor 2.86. These are different measurements, not a conflict, so not `contested`. No sample sizes, test positions or "larger extensor" and "major flexor" muscle lists are given. Weightlifter ratios are not targets for other sports.

**Example** — The lower leg shows the most extreme ratio among the best Russian weightlifters, 5.4:1, against 1.6:1 for the arms (PDF 470 / p.459).

# The Shtanga Functional Pressure Test: Blood Pressure After a Forced Breath-Hold as an Overtraining Check in Weightlifters (Ulchenko)

**What it is** — Under "Work Capacity and Functional Pressure Tests," which the book calls "an extension" of the Ch 6.2.2 tests, it describes "the cardiac function Shtanga Functional Pressure test to ascertain if the athlete is overtraining (described by Vyurberg, 1953)," regarded as "particularly suitable for athletes like Olympic weightlifters and wrestlers, whose sports require them to strain against heavy resistance" (PDF 470 / p.459, checked against the page image). Procedure: breathe in relaxed fashion for a few minutes, inhale maximally, hold "for 15-20 seconds before stopping the nose and exhaling as forcibly as possible for 2 seconds," which brings "a sharp rise in intrathoracic pressure and diminished flow of blood to the heart." Blood pressure is taken before (BP1), immediately after (BP2) and after 2 minutes of relaxed breathing (BP3). "If the contractile processes of the myocardium are normal, as in the well-prepared athlete who is not exhibiting chronic fatigue, the blood pressure decreases briefly by 5-10mm Hg." Ulchenko (1982) used it "among elite weightlifters during their specific preparation stage": Test 1, the three readings before training; Test 2, the same readings "during the most intense training loading." Grades: "1. BP decrease after Test 1 or no change after Test 2. This is regarded as an excellent reaction. 2. BP increase of up to 5mm Hg immediately after Test 2 and recovery of normal BP after 2 minutes rest. This is considered to be a good reaction. 3. BP increase of up to 7mm Hg after Test 2 and 5 minutes recovery time. This is regarded as satisfactory. 4. BP increase of 10mm Hg or more after Test 2 and prolonged elevation of BP afterwards. This is regarded as an unsatisfactory response and is associated with an overtraining state" (PDF 470 / p.459). One lifter who "reported feeling fit and strong" with low RPE scored: Test 1, BP1 130/70, BP2 140/75, BP3 135/70, a 10 mm rise "regarded as unsatisfactory"; Test 2, BP1 140/66, BP2 160/70, BP3 142/70, a 20 mm rise, also unsatisfactory. "This lifter and several others whose pressure tests were deemed to be unacceptable did not improve their results in the competition which followed," and their coaches were advised to modify training "until the pressure tests indicated a better functional state" (PDF 470 / p.459). Ulchenko "strongly advised the regular application of this pressure test," even "as an almost daily routine," and "stated that the underlying cause of this diminished functional state is certainly due to weakening of the heart's contractile ability" (PDF 471 / p.460, partly reconstructed at the right margin: "of this", "work", "weakening of", "routine to").

**Why it works** — Ulchenko's reasoning as reported: strength sports involve "straining, breath-holding and high nervous tension which, in the presence of even small disturbances in functioning of the cardiovascular system, can aggravate the situation" (PDF 470-471 / pp.459-460), and a heart with weakened contractility handles the pressure challenge worse. Inference: the rises quoted are systolic (130 to 140, 140 to 160); diastolic barely moves.

**When to apply** — The book's case: heavy strength or grappling athletes in a hard preparation block, when self-report looks fine but results stall. Read with [[principle--pair-objective-and-subjective-tests-because-rpe-can-miss-a-poor-functional-state]], which draws the book's general lesson from the same lifter.

**When NOT to apply** — `untested`: the method is described, but no sample size, comparison group or statistics are given, and the competition outcome is "this lifter and several others." The printed grading is internally loose: the text first says systolic pressure "increases significantly during the recuperation stage" and then that normal pressure "decreases briefly by 5-10mm Hg"; grade 1 mixes Test 1 and Test 2; grade 3 uses "5 minutes recovery time" though BP3 is defined at 2 minutes; and the Test 1 rise of 10 mm is called unsatisfactory although the grades are written for Test 2. Ulchenko's "certainly due to weakening of the heart's contractile ability" is a causal claim with no measure of contractility on the page. The test is a forced strain against a closed airway; the book's own caution on prolonged breath-holding for people with cardiovascular disease is in 3.4.9 ([[principle--breath-holding-and-valsalva-support-spinal-stability-in-maximal-lifting]]). Inference: a cardiovascular stress test belongs with medical staff, not as a coach-run daily screen.

**Example** — The anonymous lifter above: low RPE on clean pulls and back squats, a 20 mm systolic rise under peak loading, and no improvement at the next competition (PDF 470 / p.459).

**Related** — [[principle--pair-objective-and-subjective-tests-because-rpe-can-miss-a-poor-functional-state]], [[heuristic--heart-rate-work-capacity-tests-for-lifters]] (the Ch 6.2.2 tests this extends), [[framework--supplementary-readiness-markers-hr-bp-ceff-palpation]] (morning blood pressure as a marker), [[principle--breath-holding-and-valsalva-support-spinal-stability-in-maximal-lifting]]

# Undertraining Is Not Safe, and the Most Load an Athlete Can Survive Is Not the Optimum

**What it is** — The authors reject two opposite errors. First, the old belief of "the more training the better" or "no gain without pain," imposed "on misguided athletes either by themselves or by uninformed coaches, since they maintain that the optimum training load is the maximum training load a person can endure without injury" (PDF 471 / p.460, checked against the page image; "often", "or by" and "person can" are on the compressed right margin and are partly reconstructed). "More enlightened coaches" keep the principle "provided that a person commences training at low intensity and continually increases intensity and duration within individual limits of endurance and the time available" (PDF 471-472 / pp.460-461; "time" and "available" straddle the right margin of PDF 471 and the left margin of PDF 472, partly reconstructed). Second, the opposite belief: "It would then possibly appear as if overtraining is the sole cause of non-accidental training injuries, whereas undertraining is safe and merely leads to lack of progress. This is only partly true. Consistent undertraining, which never familiarizes the athlete with high stress levels or the so-called 'pain-barrier', may expose him to risk during the excitement of a competition. Moreover, undertraining accompanied by faulty technique, drug usage, inadequate sleep, poor nutrition or the use of unsuitable equipment can also lead to injury" (PDF 472 / p.461; the first letters of "undertraining", "which", "during" and "inadequate" are cut by the left margin and are partly reconstructed). The six injury principles on the previous page compress the point: "No stress - no progress - no injury !" (PDF 471 / p.460).

**Why it works** — The authors' mechanism is unfamiliarity: an athlete never exposed in training to the stress levels of competition meets them for the first time when the stakes and arousal are highest. Inference: this is the injury-side version of the book's adaptation argument, where avoiding stress leaves the athlete less able to cope with it.

**When to apply** — When a cautious programme keeps training loads well under what competition demands "to stay safe." Eric's review: "Recovery has to be earned by training hard first; a culture of fear grew out of early GPS/load-monitoring work that pushed teams toward under-training in the name of "recovery."" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 40, Inferred (transcript)). Eric's review: "Heavy GPS/load-monitoring data was described as having bred a "culture of fear" in the field broadly (do less, to protect recovery), which the course material argues actually leaves athletes under-prepared for competition." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 88, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: the authors and the baseline make the same argument; the authors add that it is an injury risk, not only a performance cost.

**When NOT to apply** — No injury data are given, so `untested`. In the second sentence the named risks (faulty technique, drugs, poor sleep, poor nutrition, unsuitable equipment) do the injuring; undertraining only accompanies them. Inference: the claim does not license loading past an athlete's current limits; the authors' own fix is the "enlightened" gradual increase "within individual limits." The "pain-barrier" phrase is not defined.

**Example** — The authors' case: an athlete who has trained consistently below competition stress "may" be exposed to risk "during the excitement of a competition" (PDF 472 / p.461).

# Train for a Safety Factor Above Competition Forces, but Strength and Bulk Alone Do Not Protect an Inefficient Athlete

**What it is** — Under "Pattern Deviations and Safety Factors," Siff (in 7.5 the book says "the author" gave the 1989 NSCA presentation (Siff, 1989), PDF p. 429 / printed p. 418, and that "An overview of this presentation and workshop acted as the basis for Chapter 7.2 above", PDF p. 430 / printed p. 419) writes that PNF patterns "were devised for rehabilitation, not elite sporting training, so that it is not incorrect to employ patterns of movement which may deviate significantly from those stipulated in PNF" (italics in the original). PNF keeps patterns "close to the body, a situation which occurs seldom in sport," where "forceful or rapid movements have to be executed with the distal extremities far from the relevant joints, thereby imposing large torque on these joints. If training always ensures that this degree of torque or force is avoided, then it will not prepare the athlete for the rigors of the sport and will increase susceptibility to overtraining and injury." Hence: "As in engineering, one must plan for a certain safety factor which allows the athlete to manage even larger forces than those which may be encountered in competition. For example, a safety factor of 1.2 means that a system can cope with a maximal loading of 0.2 or 20% greater than normally expected." Heavy supplementary resistance training ("cross training") serves this, "provided that it does not alter the neuromuscular patterns needed in the given sport." The limit: "Far too many athletes (e.g. in football and rugby) believe that increase in strength and bodymass will automatically protect them from injury. If one executes a movement in an inefficient manner or reacts too slowly to produce adequate force, then even gigantic strength or structural bulk can be inadequate to prevent injury." (All PDF p. 421 / printed p. 410, checked against the page image.)

**Why it works** — Siff gives the engineering analogy and one sentence of reasoning: "high levels of skill and reactive ability in sport are vital in ensuring that sporting action is efficient and safe" (PDF p. 421 / printed p. 410). No physiological mechanism or data are given. Inference: the claim has two parts, tissue capacity above expected load (the safety factor) and timing and skill to apply it (reactive ability), and the book makes both necessary and neither sufficient.

**When to apply** — When an exercise is rejected because it loads a joint at long lever arms, ask whether the sport imposes that torque; if it does, graded exposure is preparation, not risk. When a football player or coach treats added mass as injury armour, use the second half of the passage. Eric's baseline: "Injury risk is reduced, not eliminated, through sound progression of load, training means, and density, in collaboration with Athletic Medicine" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 140, Inferred (transcript + slides)); and "an athlete who can bench 400 lb but can't do 10 clean push-ups has "something out of whack" that needs fixing regardless of their strength numbers." (line 141, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: both baseline lines and Siff's passage refuse to equate raw strength with protection.

**When NOT to apply** — The 1.2 figure is an engineering illustration, not a measured training target: the book gives no way to measure "forces ... encountered in competition" for a given athlete or joint, and no data that a 20% margin lowers injury. Heavy supplementary work is endorsed only if it "does not alter the neuromuscular patterns needed in the given sport" (PDF p. 421 / printed p. 410). Exposure to large torques still has to be progressive; Eric's baseline line 142 treats "abrupt, large changes" as "a direct injury-risk driver, not just a training-quality issue" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 142, Inferred (transcript)).

**Example** — Siff's own: football and rugby players who believe "increase in strength and bodymass will automatically protect them from injury" (PDF p. 421 / printed p. 410). Inference: a lineman whose squat rises 20 kg over an off-season but whose reaction to a cut block is slow is not protected by the squat alone; the book does not give this case.

# Nine General Biomechanical Causes of Injury, Expanded Into Eighteen Specific Causes

**What it is** — Under "General Biomechanical Causes of Injury" (PDF 476 / p.465, checked against the page image), nine general causes: "1. The force or stress component (force per unit area of tissue) on some part of the body is excessive in a particular direction (this may be caused by very large mass or very large acceleration); 2. The torque or moment about a certain pivot or joint is excessive; 3. Momentum is too great to be adequately utilised or dissipated; 4. The work load or energy involved over a given period is excessive; 5. The power generated by the muscles is excessive at a particular instant; 6. The strain (change in relative length, ΔL/L) in any tissues is excessive; 7. The mechanical properties of any given tissues are inadequate to handle the loading; 8. The Rate of Force Development (RFD) is excessive at a particular instant; 9. Frictional forces are too large (mat burns or jerkiness) or too small (slipping)." These "may be expanded to identify some more specific causes," 18 bullets: inappropriate warming up or stretching; inappropriate or inefficient patterns of movement; unsafe use of momentum; excessive range of movement for a particular joint; inappropriate phases of muscular tension or relaxation; use of inappropriate soft tissues for a particular action; acceleration or deceleration too great; an excessive load on any part of the body; inappropriate sequences of exercises; excessive exertion during exhaustion, distress, illness or injury; inadequate rest, recovery time or methods of recuperation; inappropriate or faulty equipment; excessive impact forces on body parts making contact with an object or surface; "Inappropriate or inefficient breathing patterns"; excessive duration of any activity; inability to interpret and use proprioceptive and other sensory feedback; inability to "visualize, predict or use feedforward"; and "Inefficient use of breathing or breath-holding patterns" (PDF 476 / p.465; the bullets are paraphrased except where quoted). The left margin of PDF 476 cuts the first letter of a few lines ("The general", "These general"); no list item is affected.

**Why it works** — The general list is mechanics: each item is a physical quantity (stress, torque, momentum, work, power, strain, RFD, friction) or the tissue's capacity to bear it. Inference: the specific list maps programme and coaching choices onto those quantities; for example, poor exercise sequencing or inadequate rest raises the work and fatigue items, and faulty technique shifts stress, torque or strain to the wrong tissue.

**When to apply** — As a checklist when reviewing an injury or a drill: name which physical quantity was excessive, or which tissue was inadequate, before naming the programme cause. Inference: items 5 and 8 (power and RFD "excessive at a particular instant") are a reminder that explosive training carries its own injury mechanism, separate from heavy load.

**When NOT to apply** — Lists with no data or ranking, so `untested`. Two specific bullets nearly repeat each other ("Inappropriate or inefficient breathing patterns" and "Inefficient use of breathing or breath-holding patterns"); Inference: the 18 are really 17 distinct items. Inference: the general list names mechanisms that can be computed only in a lab; in the field it works as a vocabulary, not a measurement.

**Example** — General item 9 in both directions: friction "too large (mat burns or jerkiness) or too small (slipping)" (PDF 476 / p.465).

**Related** — [[heuristic--ten-causes-of-deviation-from-normal-movement-patterns]], [[framework--six-fundamental-principles-of-the-injury-process]], [[claim--overtraining-injury-parallels-engineering-fatigue-from-overload-and-overuse]]

# Six Strength-Training Causes of Overtraining Injury to Check First

**What it is** — The authors' list: "In the case of strength training, overtraining injuries may be the result of too many repetitions or sets, regular training with near maximum loads, training the same muscle groups too frequently, inadequate recovery periods, insufficient rest or faulty execution of any movement" (PDF 454 / p.443, checked against the page image). Six causes: (1) too many repetitions or sets; (2) regular training with near-maximum loads; (3) training the same muscle groups too frequently; (4) inadequate recovery periods; (5) insufficient rest; (6) faulty execution of any movement.

**Why it works** — The page gives the list without a mechanism. Inference: causes 1-5 are dose (volume, intensity, frequency, and recovery between and outside sessions) and cause 6 is technique, so the list splits a strength-room injury into "too much" versus "done wrong," which point to different fixes.

**When to apply** — As an audit sequence when a lifter develops an overuse complaint or a local overtraining picture (see [[heuristic--tell-general-from-local-overtraining-and-acute-from-chronic]]): check sets and reps, the share of near-maximal work, how often the same group is hit, rest between sessions, rest outside training, and technique. Eric's review: "Tracy Fober's maxim ("use a barbell like a chisel, not a sledgehammer") is adopted as a guiding standard: prioritize movement quality and confidence-through-competence over chasing hypertrophy or 1RM numbers, especially early in a training cycle." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 109, Inferred (transcript + slides)). Inference: that maxim addresses causes 2 and 6 directly.

**When NOT to apply** — No data, no thresholds and no ranking among the six; the list says what "may" cause injury. "Inadequate recovery periods" and "insufficient rest" overlap and the book does not separate them. The 8.2 discussion splits overtraining injuries into "overload injuries (caused by too large a load at any instant) and overuse injuries (caused by very frequent application of a given load)" (PDF 438 / p.427; see [[claim--plyometric-injury-risk-comes-from-prescription-not-the-method]]). Inference: cause 2 maps mainly to overload and causes 1 and 3 to overuse; the 8.5 list does not make that mapping itself.

**Example** — Inference, applied: a lifter benching heavy four days a week who reports shoulder soreness that persists through rest days shows causes 2 and 3 at once; cutting near-maximal sessions to one and the bench frequency to two is the first test, before any treatment.

**Related** — [[claim--overtraining-is-accumulated-stress-adaptation-imbalance-exhaustion-is-short-term]], [[claim--plyometric-injury-risk-comes-from-prescription-not-the-method]], [[principle--find-the-optimum-stress-level-rather-than-avoiding-stress]]

# Before Cueing a Faulty Movement Pattern, Check the Ten Things That Make Patterns Deviate

**What it is** — "With particular reference to injuries produced by inefficient patterns of movement, one must appreciate that deviations from normal patterns may be caused by:" (PDF 476 / p.465, checked against the page image) "Pain, soreness, stiffness or discomfort"; "Muscle weakness or imbalance between muscle groups"; "Any limitation in the range of joint range of movement in any direction"; "Uncoordinated movement"; "Musculoskeletal changes"; "Fatigue"; "Changes in surface, footwear, equipment or environment"; "Neural changes"; "Visual or balance changes"; "Emotional disturbance" (PDF 476-477 / pp.465-466).

**Why it works** — The authors give the list without a mechanism. Inference: a movement pattern is the output of the body's current state, so a fault seen today may be the athlete compensating for pain, fatigue, a range limit or new shoes rather than a skill error; cueing the fault without removing the cause asks the athlete to override a compensation.

**When to apply** — When a well-learned pattern changes, especially suddenly, ask about these ten before coaching technique. Inference: the first and sixth items (pain and fatigue) are the most common in a team setting and are the ones the next pages tie to injury: pain can reflexly inhibit muscles ([[claim--pain-and-minor-knee-injury-reflexly-inhibit-quadriceps-strength]]).

**When NOT to apply** — A list without data or priorities, so `untested`. "Neural changes" and "Musculoskeletal changes" are broad enough to cover almost anything. A novice's faulty pattern is usually a skill that is not yet learned, which the list does not include.

**Example** — Inference: a sprinter whose stride changes the week the team moves to a new surface; the list's "Changes in surface, footwear, equipment or environment" (PDF 477 / p.466) comes before any cue.

**Related** — [[framework--nine-general-biomechanical-causes-of-injury-and-eighteen-specific-causes]], [[claim--pain-and-minor-knee-injury-reflexly-inhibit-quadriceps-strength]], [[claim--pain-is-an-unreliable-guide-to-injury-and-exercise-safety]]

# Pain, and Even Painless Minor Knee Injury, Can Reflexly Inhibit the Quadriceps and Cut Strength

**What it is** — "However, it should be noted that the perception of pain by the central nervous system (CNS) can reorganise the motor control system to minimise the pain, which can result in reflex inhibition of the muscles to exert maximal strength and thereby lead to muscle weakness (Stokes & Young, 1984). In fact, even if the injury is not accompanied by pain, this can also occur. This is very common with even relatively insubstantial injuries of the knee such as patellar tendinitis, peripatellar pain syndrome or chondromalacia patellae, which significantly reduce the ability of the quadriceps to produce powerful contraction" (PDF 477 / p.466, checked against the page image; "reorganise", "exert", "is not", "of the" and "reduce" sit on the compressed right margin and are partly reconstructed). A second, hedged claim follows: "It is possible that the pain caused by muscle swelling or delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS) may also provoke the CNS into responding with alternative motor programs which distribute force production over a larger number of muscle fibres and diminish the efficiency and magnitude of strength output (Stauber, 1989). The importance of dealing with even minor pain, soreness or injury then becomes obvious" (PDF 477 / p.466).

**Why it works** — The book's mechanism: the CNS reorganises motor control to protect the painful or injured part, inhibiting maximal voluntary contraction. Inference: that this happens "even if the injury is not accompanied by pain" means the trigger is the injury itself, not only the pain, so pain-free does not mean inhibition-free.

**When to apply** — In return to play after knee problems: expect quadriceps weakness that is reflexive, not only disuse, and test strength before assuming it is back. Inference: the modern term for the knee case is arthrogenic muscle inhibition; check current literature before relying on the 1984 citation.

**When NOT to apply** — Stokes & Young (1984) and Stauber (1989) are cited, not described, so `untested` on this page. The DOMS point is explicitly speculative ("It is possible that ... may"), and should not be cited as a finding. "Very common" is not quantified. The page gives no rule for how long inhibition lasts or how to reverse it.

**Example** — The book's own: patellar tendinitis, peripatellar pain syndrome or chondromalacia patellae, "relatively insubstantial injuries of the knee," which "significantly reduce the ability of the quadriceps to produce powerful contraction" (PDF 477 / p.466).

# Seven Factors That Limit Strength Production

**What it is** — Strength output in the short and long term is limited by seven
interacting factors: **trainability** (genetic ceiling for hypertrophy, fibre-type
distribution, leverage, and pre-training status); **neuromuscular efficiency** (skill in
recruiting the right muscles accurately and powerfully); **biomechanical efficiency**
(leverage and relative muscle-group strength, trainable unlike raw genetic trainability);
**psychological factors** (motivation, focus, pain tolerance, perceived exertion, coach
influence); **pain and fear of pain** (distinguishing injury pain, a protective signal to
act on, from effort pain, a subjective load-intensity signal usable via an RPE-style
scale); **injury and fear of injury** (reflex inhibition of contraction around a damaged
joint is well documented; return to top performance depends on the athlete's own
perception that rehab is complete, not just medical clearance); and **fatigue** (central
vs. peripheral, discussed further in
[[framework--central-vs-peripheral-fatigue-mechanisms]]). (PDF pp. 23-25, printed pp.
12-14.)

**Why it works** — Strength testing and training programs typically control for load,
volume, and technique, but this list makes explicit that psychological state, injury
history, and perceived pain/fear operate as real physiological limiters on force output.
Reflex inhibition around an injured joint is stated in the text as "a well-known phenomenon
which produces muscle weakness when a joint is damaged" (Stokes & Young, 1984; printed 14).
Inference: this is not just a "mental" factor layered on top of a physical ceiling, but a
measurable neuromuscular effect, not a motivation problem.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** usable as a checklist when an athlete's force output
underperforms their apparent physical capacity: before assuming a physical/programming
cause, rule out fear of re-injury, unaddressed effort-pain tolerance, or psychological
state. The authors state "return to top level performance will occur only if the
athlete perceives rehabilitation to be complete" and the fear of pain or re-injury being
minimal (PDF p. 25, printed p. 14). **Eric's baseline:** Applied Performance's stated role
in return-to-performance is to supply information supporting Athletic Performance's and
Athletic Medicine's RTP decisions, a support/advisory role rather than a final-decision
role (`method-baseline.md`, "Rehab and return to play," citing
`baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.6`); that same baseline section is flagged as
"the thinnest discipline in the corpus" with no stated RTP criteria or battery.
**Inference:** the authors' fear-of-injury/pain framing is a plausible partial fill for
that documented gap, though neither source states this connection directly.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a descriptive taxonomy, not a measurement
protocol; none of these seven factors have a given cutoff or test threshold in this section
of the text (PDF pp. 23-25, printed pp. 12-14). **Inference:** do not use "fear of injury"
as a catch-all explanation without other supporting evidence (movement quality, self-report,
clinical input from Athletic Medicine); reflex inhibition and psychological guarding can
look similar from the outside. This caution is this entry's own judgment, not stated in the
text.

**Example** — **Inference:** An athlete cleared medically after an ACL reconstruction who still shows
reduced force output on the operated leg during testing may be exhibiting reflex inhibition
and/or fear of re-injury, not a residual physical deficit alone; that changes what the
next intervention should target.

**Related** — [[framework--central-vs-peripheral-fatigue-mechanisms]].

# There Is No Single "Optimal" Quadriceps:Hamstring Ratio: It Changes With Sport, Joint Angle and Test Velocity

**What it is** — It is often claimed the optimal quadriceps-to-hamstring strength ratio is
60:40, but Russian scientists found this ratio depends on the specific sport (Vorobyev,
1978): they "determined that this ratio (measured when knee extension torque is greatest)
should be nearer 80:20 for weightlifters and jumpers," while a treadmill-movement
measurement gives runners a ratio of approximately 50:50. A related popular belief, that
injuries are far more common once left/right lower-extremity strength differs by more than
10%, is also questioned. The authors cite "recent research" finding that neither
recommendation is supported by scientifically controlled experiments that correct torque
outputs for the effect of gravity and avoid stretching the hamstrings (Stephens & Reid,
1988). The flexor/extensor-ratio recommendation is additionally vague because the ratio
varies across the joint's range of motion. Verified against the page image (Fig 4.16, PDF p.
245, printed p. 234): the figure plots the ratio of isokinetic knee-extensor to knee-flexor
torque (y-axis 0.5 to 3.5) against joint angle at 36, 108 and 180 degrees/second, from
Cybex dynamometer data; the caption gives no source and no population, and states that
"joint angle varies between partial knee flexion in the seated position to full extension
at 90 degrees." The text reads the figure: the ratio at the knee at 80 degrees (in Fig 4.16's
convention, where 90 degrees is full extension, so near full extension) is about 75:25 at 36
degrees/second (a ratio of 3.0) but 68:32 at 180 degrees/second (about 2.1). The figure does
not match the text's first value: at the 80-degree tick the 36 degrees/second curve reads
about 2.7 (roughly 73:27) and reaches 3.0 only near 88-90 degrees, while the 180
degrees/second curve reads about 2.2 (checked against the page image, PDF p. 245); the text
does not reconcile the two;
the ratio equals the traditional 60:40 figure (1.5) only at approximately 50 degrees. Since
the ratio changes with both joint angle and measurement velocity, the authors conclude "it
is meaningless to prescribe an optimal ratio for any joint," and it would be more relevant
to refer to a characteristic curve over a full range of movement for a given angular
velocity. The page is internally inconsistent: it reports Vorobyev's sport-specific targets
(80:20, 50:50) as what the ratio "should be," then calls any optimal ratio "meaningless"
(both PDF p. 244, printed p. 233). (PDF pp. 244-245, printed pp. 233-234, "4.2.6.2
Limitations of the Isokinetic Method," "Recommended Strength Ratios," Fig 4.16.)

**Why it works** — The authors give no physiological mechanism for why the ratio shifts with
sport, joint angle or velocity. Their argument is empirical: the figure shows the ratio
changing across angle and velocity, so a single number cannot describe it. Inference: a
single-number ratio averages over torque variation that differs between the extensors and
flexors across the range and across contraction speed.

**When to apply** — Use this as a caution against citing a single flexor/extensor or
left/right strength-ratio target (e.g. "60:40 quad:hamstring," "no more than 10% L/R
difference") as universally optimal or diagnostic of injury risk. If a ratio must be used,
specify the joint angle, the angle convention and the angular velocity it was measured at,
and prefer a full-range characteristic curve over a single number when data allow, per the
authors.

Eric's baseline: NordBord hamstring testing is "explicitly retained for smaller, targeted
return-to-play groups paired with joint-specific isometric testing (ForceFrame-style)"
(`method-baseline.md`, Rehab and return to play); the corpus sets no flexor/extensor ratio
target.

Inference: this section bears on how such ratio data are read for return-to-play decisions.

**When NOT to apply** — Fig 4.16 is uncited Cybex data at 36, 108 and 180 degrees/second on
an unspecified population; Vorobyev (1978) supplies the sport-specific ratios and Stephens &
Reid (1988) the gravity-correction critique. The specific ratio-versus-angle values should
not be treated as universal constants for every athlete or joint. Inference: the figure's
convention (90 degrees = full extension) is the reverse of the common 0 degrees = extension
convention, so its angles cannot be compared directly with most modern reports. Do
not use this entry to conclude ratio testing is worthless; the claim is that a single
"optimal ratio" number is misleading, not that ratio measurement itself carries no
information (see [[claim--natural-asymmetry-caution-against-isokinetic-symmetry-correction]]
for the related but distinct caution about using isokinetic ratios to drive "correction").
Inference: the Vorobyev targets were measured at a named point (greatest knee-extension
torque), which partly meets the authors' angle objection but not their velocity objection.

**Example** — Inference: a rehabilitation report citing "this athlete's quad:hamstring ratio
is below the healthy 60:40 standard" should specify the joint angle and test velocity the
ratio was measured at, since per Fig 4.16 the same limb could show a ratio above 60:40 at
one angle/velocity and at or below it at another.

**Related** — [[claim--natural-asymmetry-caution-against-isokinetic-symmetry-correction]]
(Ch3.3.4.4, a related caution against using isokinetic ratios to "correct" asymmetry),
[[heuristic--isokinetic-testing-limitations-for-functional-sport-specificity]],
[[claim--pursuing-perfect-bilateral-symmetry-can-be-counterproductive]].

**Also in 8.7** — The 60:40 ratio comes back with isometric data for Olympic weightlifters: extensors 11.51 ± 1.78 and flexors 4.02 ± 0.69 per kg bodymass, extensors on average 2.86 times stronger, and among the best Russian lifters arms 1.6:1, trunk 4.3:1, thighs 4.3:1 and lower leg 5.4:1 (Vorobyev, 1978; PDF 469-470 / pp.458-459). These are isometric, whole-body figures, a different measure from the isokinetic 80:20 knee figure above, so not a conflict. See [[claim--weightlifter-extensor-flexor-strength-ratios-far-exceed-the-1-5-norm]].

# Some Movement Asymmetry Is Natural and Safe; Chasing Perfect Bilateral Symmetry Can Backfire

**What it is** — Because of genuine structural and functional body asymmetry, a single
"correct," perfectly symmetric technique enforced on every athlete "may seriously diminish
an athlete's performance." In lifting, the bar routinely rotates or tilts slightly to one
side rather than traveling perfectly parallel to the frontal/sagittal/transverse planes,
and this is described as natural rather than a flaw to eliminate: coaches should learn to
distinguish natural, harmless asymmetry from genuinely inefficient or unsafe deviation, in
part by observing and recording bar trajectory from both sides of the body and comparing it
to the ideal trajectory, rather than assuming any visible asymmetry is a problem. The text
explicitly cautions that **relying on isokinetic or similar devices to measure
agonist/antagonist or left/right strength ratios in order to "correct" so-called imbalances
"may be unproductive and ill-advised."** (PDF p. 166, printed p. 155, "3.3.4.4
Strength, Symmetry and Limb Alignment"; symmetric training itself is deferred to Ch4.2.8.)

**Why it works** — No formal mechanism is given beyond the general point that
individualized body structure, muscle composition, and neuromuscular control make a
uniform symmetric ideal biomechanically unrealistic for many athletes. **Inference:** a
further reason, not stated in this section, is that isokinetic symmetry testing measures an
isolated, single-joint proxy that may not represent functional, whole-movement asymmetry
accurately or usefully.

**When to apply** — Use this as a caution before flagging or "correcting" an athlete's
L/R asymmetry purely because a test shows a numeric difference: first establish, via
technique observation (e.g. bar-path video from both sides), whether the asymmetry is a
natural individual pattern or an actual inefficiency/injury-risk deviation.

**When NOT to apply** — Direct tension with current Baylor practice: this claim sits in
tension with the department's own testing framework: the HD ODSF metric-selection model
lists symmetry (L/R differences) as an *optional* force-plate reporting category
(`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring," citing
`hd-odsf-metrics.md`), and joint-specific isometric testing (ForceFrame-style) is retained
for targeted return-to-play groups (`method-baseline.md`, citing
`2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md`). The baseline does not itself say symmetry
indices *drive* RTP decisions, only that they are collected as an optional category and
that joint-specific testing continues for RTP groups; this entry should not be read as
claiming the baseline directly contradicts the book on that specific point. **Eric's review
would be needed** to reconcile this 1990s-2009-era caution against isokinetic-symmetry-based
"correction" with the department's practice: the book's objection is specifically to
*using an isokinetic ratio to drive a correction*, which is a narrower target than symmetry
monitoring for tracking purposes more broadly. Modern literature is itself split on how
symmetry data should be used: Afonso et al
([[research-papers/afonso-undated-asymmetries-and-injury-risk-when-titles-spin-the-tale]])
and Bishop 2016
([[research-papers/bishop-2016-asymmetries-of-the-lower-limb-the-calculation-conundrum-in-strength-training-and-condition]])
both caution against naive asymmetry-correction approaches, while Callaway 2026
([[research-papers/callaway-2026-group-normative-data-and-arbitrary-asymmetry-thresholds-fail-to-represent-individual-playe]])
argues group-normative asymmetry thresholds fail to
represent individual players, a related but distinct caution about the metric itself
rather than about correcting it.

**Example** — **Inference:** a force-plate report showing a 12% L/R asymmetry in a healthy,
high-performing athlete with no injury history or technique flaw, per this claim, is not
automatically something to "fix": the text would ask whether that asymmetry reflects a
natural, individual movement pattern before prescribing corrective unilateral work.

subsection, same overall posture-and-technique section); [[claim--pursuing-perfect-bilateral-symmetry-can-be-counterproductive]] (Ch4.2.8 "The Concept
of Symmetric Training", the section the text itself deferred to).
